sources.title: Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump
sources.note: UNESCO synthesis of nearly six millennia of communal bison hunting, drive lanes, stratified bone beds and processing camps.

sources.title: Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump, Parks Canada
sources.note: Official account of cairns, meat caches, cooking pits and the uses of bison meat, hide, sinew, bone, horn and dung.

sources.title: Old Women's Buffalo Jump National Historic Site
sources.note: Official archaeological chronology and interpretation of Pelican Lake, Besant, communal work, preservation and ritual.

sources.title: Prehistoric and Protohistoric Overview of the White River Badlands
sources.note: NPS scholarly regional overview of Besant, Avonlea, ceramics, bow hunting and changing social relations.

sources.title: Archeological Significance of Yellowstone Lake
sources.note: NPS archaeology of atlatls, later bows, pottery, hearths and stone circles at a Plains and mountain margin.

sources.title: American Indian Culture at Tallgrass Prairie
sources.note: NPS synthesis of exchange, ceramics, domesticated plants, bow hunting and later horticultural villages in the eastern Plains.

sources.title: Bison Kill Sites in South Dakota, 9000 B.C. to 1875 A.D.
sources.note: National Register research context on bison behavior, kill sites, Plains Village horticulture, storage and fortification.

sources.title: America's Grasslands: Great Plains and Pothole Prairies
sources.note: USGS ecological overview of rainfall gradients, prairie potholes and grassland animals.

sources.title: Ungulate Migrations of the Western United States: Bison
sources.note: USGS scientific account of bison size, forage preferences, spring green-up and herd movement.

sources.title: Interpretation and compendium of historical fire accounts in the Northern Great Plains
sources.note: Federal research on historically documented Indigenous fire use, seasonality, gathering and hunting.

sources.title: Texas: Alibates Flint Quarries National Monument
sources.note: NPS archaeology of more than 700 quarries, stone-tool production, long-distance exchange and Plains Village settlements.

sources.title: Antelope Creek Culture, 1150 to 1450 CE
sources.note: NPS site-specific account of southern Plains houses, springs, mixed farming and hunting, exchange and evidence of conflict.

sources.title: Earthlodge at Knife River Indian Villages
sources.note: NPS account of later Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara earthlodges, construction, household space, storage and sacred meaning.

sources.title: Knife River: Early Village Life on the Plains
sources.note: NPS synthesis of later northern Plains agriculture, women, matrilineal landholding, storytelling, play, dance and ritual.

sources.title: The Plains Indians
sources.note: NPS warning that more than thirty historically documented Plains peoples differed in language, religion, mobility and farming.

sources.title: Travel, A Song for the Horse Nation
sources.note: National Museum of the American Indian material on dog and later horse travois, camp movement and women carrying household goods.

sources.title: Paleo and Archaic Cultures at Great Sand Dunes
sources.note: NPS account of early regional gatherings, family groups, teaching, plant knowledge and a Smithsonian-excavated bison camp.

sources.title: Bison Carcass Utilization at Kill Sites from the Great Plains
sources.note: Canadian Archaeological Association study of marrow, grease and variable processing choices at kill sites.

sources.title: Observations on Butchering at a Prehistoric Montana Bison Kill
sources.note: Peer-reviewed bone analysis of transport decisions, marrow extraction and thorough carcass use.

sources.title: Fat Content in Bison Leg Bones and Applications to Archaeology
sources.note: Experimental archaeological study of bone grease yields and the effects of grease rendering on bone assemblages.

sources.title: Bonebeds and other myths on the Great Plains
sources.note: Scholarly warning that spectacular bison bone beds are only a small and unusually visible share of Plains sites.

sources.title: Health conditions before Columbus
sources.note: Peer-reviewed overview of what bones and teeth can and cannot reveal about precontact North American health.

sources.title: Archaeological Perspectives on Warfare on the Great Plains
sources.note: University Press of Colorado synthesis of sparse early evidence, trauma, defenses and changing conflict evidence.

sources.title: Writing-on-Stone / Aisinai'pi
sources.note: UNESCO account of Blackfoot sacred landscape, dated archaeology, rock art and cultural continuity.

sources.title: Aisinai'pi National Historic Site of Canada
sources.note: Official Blackfoot-centered interpretation of vision quests, biographical scenes and continuing spiritual meaning.

sources.title: Olsen-Chubbuck Collection
sources.note: University of Colorado Museum archive documenting excavation and a large Paleoindian bison drive system.

sources.title: Twenty-five Years of the Cooper Site
sources.note: University of Oklahoma Archeological Survey account of stratified kills, sourced stone and a painted bison skull.

sources.title: Archaeology on the Great Plains
sources.note: University Press of Kansas scholarly synthesis stressing five Plains regions, mobile hunters, farmers and cultural continuity.

proposedOverrides.summary: Broad pre-horse Great Plains atlas umbrella for diverse hunters, gatherers, farmers and villagers; never one people or language.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact indexed display name is “Plain bison hunters”; the singular wording is preserved rather than silently corrected.
The polygon is a broad imported atlas umbrella, not one self-named people, language, state or archaeological culture.
The record mixes mobile hunters, seasonal gathering places, horticultural villages, river settlements and regional archaeological traditions.
The feature is absent in 2000 BCE, appears in 1500 BCE, changes along neighboring layers, vanishes at 1492, returns as a two-part multipolygon at 1500 and is absent at 1530.
The crowded 1492 and 1530 point-owner labels are atlas taxonomy seams and include questionable synchrony; they are not endorsed as precise territories.
Later ethnographic and historic examples are labeled comparisons and never projected unchanged across the full target interval.
The target is predominantly pre-horse; the iconic mounted Plains world developed mainly after this card closes.
Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is securely attributable to this atlas record. Rock art is not recast as a target-wide deciphered script.
